contributions.headingText: Clear cell odontogenic carcinoma (CCOdC) is an odontogenic carcinoma characterized by sheets, nests, or cords of clear cells in a fibrocellular or hyalinized stroma.
2B5J & XH5DZ4 Malignant miscellaneous tumours of bone or articular cartilage of other or unspecified sites & Clear cell odontogenic carcinoma
Not recommended: clear cell odontogenic tumour; clear cell ameloblastoma.
All CCOdCs develop in the jaws. Three quarters of cases arise in the mandible, most frequently in the posterior body and lower ramus {31482399}.

The clinical manifestations are nonspecific, with destructive jaw swelling with or without pain, paraesthesia, and tooth mobility, and later with ulceration to the mucosa. Less commonly, patients develop lymphadenopathy (19%) or distant metastases (11%).

Imaging

Radiographically, CCOdCs are expansile, poorly defined radiolucencies often exhibiting tooth root resorption {31482399}.
More than 100 cases of CCOdC have been reported in the literature, with a mean age at presentation of 53 years, and with 63% of cases in female patients {31227275}.

EWSR1 rearrangements have been reported in > 80% of cases {23715163}. ATF1 is the most common fusion partner, and CREB1 and CREM are less frequent {23715163; 30047065; 33616852}. CCOdCs are morphologically and immunohistochemically similar to salivary gland hyalinizing clear cell carcinomas, which share the EWSR1 translocation, suggesting a common pathogenesis {21484932}.
CCOdC is an intraosseous tumour with a homogeneous, tan-white cut surface; indistinct borders; and sometimes soft tissue extension.

CCOdCs are composed of lobular sheets, nests, or trabeculae of monomorphic, polygonal cells with clear to slightly eosinophilic cytoplasm and eccentric nuclei embedded in a hyalinized or fibrocellular stroma {4077550}. Peripheral palisading may or may not be present, and the tumour may have a heterogeneous appearance, with areas of more basaloid epithelium without cytoplasmic clearing. The clear cells are negative for mucin, but they are PAS-positive and diastase-sensitive, indicating glycogen. The mitotic index is low, and some CCOdCs are bland and relatively indolent. Necrosis and angiolymphatic invasion are uncommon, but perineural invasion is reported in one third of tumours {21290202}.

Immunohistochemistry

CCOdCs are positive for cytokeratins (AE1/AE3, CK5/6, CK19), p63, and EMA, but they are negative for myoepithelial markers (SMA, calponin, and S100 {21290202; 31482399}).

Differential diagnosis

The differential diagnosis includes other clear cell–rich gnathic neoplasms, including other odontogenic tumours (clear cell calcifying epithelial odontogenic tumour, amyloid subtype of odontogenic fibroma), salivary tumours, both metastatic and intraosseous primary neoplasms (mucoepidermoid carcinoma, epithelial-myoepithelial carcinoma), and metastatic neoplasms (renal cell carcinoma, melanoma) {32642935}. Odontogenic carcinoma with dentinoid has overlapping morphological features, with some cases having a clear cell phenotype, but these form dentinoid and appear to be a distinct entity {25409850}.
EWSR1 rearrangement facilitates diagnosis but is technically challenging due to specimen decalcification.

Essential: location in jaws; prominent clear cell phenotype; infiltrative margin; hyalinized or fibrocellular stroma.

Desirable: EWSR1 translocation.

Although there is no defined eighth-edition Union for International Cancer Control (UICC) / American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) TNM staging system staging guidance, the use of International Collaboration on Cancer Reporting (ICCR) minimum data set reporting is encouraged {30500289}.

Primary management is complete surgical resection. The role of adjuvant therapy is not clearly defined. The prognosis is variable, with a local recurrence rate of nearly 40% {31482399}. Metastases have been reported to cervical lymph nodes, and (uncommonly) to the lungs and bone, and may occur after many years. Approximately 11% of patients succumb to the disease {31227275}.
